newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu to decide on building in East Jerusalem.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu to decide on building in East Jerusalem.

text.p: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu vowed on Monday to strengthen Israel's hold over all of Jerusalem, saying he would decide within days whether to build a new Jewish neighbourhood in the Arab east of the city.

Netanyahu returned from a U.S. visit to face political trouble at home from critics who accused him of promising U.S. President Bill Clinton to freeze plans to construct 6,500 housing units at the Har Homa site.

Jerusalem Mayor Ehud Olmert said he would send bulldozers to Har Homa within days to pave the way for construction if Israeli media reports proved true that Netanyahu had effectively killed the project.

"I am simply incredulous over the things I am hearing here. Someone is trying to grab headlines over nothing...Is there anyone here who does not intend to build, pave roads or develop Jerusalem?" Netanyahu told reporters.
"I intend to convene the ministerial committee on Jerusalem for two meetings in the coming days and take all the necessary decisions," he said, referring to the Har Homa project.
Netanyahu, who chairs the committee, said the decisions would "better reflect our absolute commitment to Israeli sovereignty in Jerusalem in all parts of the city".
Israel Radio said the committee would meet on Tuesday.

The Peace Now movement -- an opponent of Jewish settlement on land captured from the Arabs in the 1967 Middle East war -- said building on Har Homa, a hill of pine forests near the Arab village Sur Bahir, would ignite Arab violence.

"Har Homa would be another Jerusalem tunnel," Peace Now spokesman Mossi Raz said, referring to Israeli-Palestinian clashes last September following Israel's opening of a new entrance to a tourist tunnel near Moslem holy sites in the city.
The violence, which threatened to wreck the Israel-PLO peace process, claimed the lives of 61 Palestinians and 15 Israelis.
Netanyahu could face a revolt in his own Likud party and from rightist coalition partners if the project does not go ahead.
"I see this issue of Har Homa as a watershed," Olmert said.

"This government exists on the basis of a parliamentary majority and I find it difficult to believe there will be a majority for a policy that does not fulfil detailed commitments on Jerusalem," he told Israel Radio.

Binyamin Begin, a member of the Likud who quit the cabinet over the government's handover of most of the West Bank town of Hebron to the PLO last month, accused the Israeli leader of "dividing Jerusalem".
Netanyahu used the phrase as his rallying cry in defeating Labour Prime Minister Shimon Peres in last year's national election.

The PLO claims Arab East Jerusalem as the capital of a future Palestininan state and has warned Netanyahu not to take any action in the city that would prejudice talks slated to begin next month on a permanent peace settlement.
The Har Homa controversy dominated news reports in Israel on Monday and overshadowed Israeli-PLO talks on implementing interim agreements signed since a landmark peace deal in 1993.
Israeli and Palestinian teams met at a Jerusalem hotel to discuss civilian issues such as the environment and procedures at international entry points into self-ruled areas of the West Bank and Gaza.
